terms.definition: AWS's fully managed, scalable object storage service. Stores data as objects inside containers called buckets, accessible from anywhere via a unique URL.
terms.example: Storing website images, backups, or log files that need to be accessed globally.

terms.definition: The top-level container in S3 for storing objects. Created in a specific AWS region and must have a globally unique name across all AWS accounts.
terms.example: Creating a bucket called 'mycompany-backups-2025' in ap-south-1 to store database backups.

terms.definition: A file stored in S3, consisting of the actual data plus metadata (owner, size, storage class, timestamps). Identified by its unique key within a bucket.
terms.example: A JPEG image, a ZIP backup file, or a CSV report stored in an S3 bucket.

terms.definition: The unique name (path) that identifies an object within an S3 bucket. Equivalent to a filename, and can include folder-like path separators.
terms.example: The key 'reports/2025/november/sales.csv' identifies a specific file within a bucket.

terms.definition: The unique web address for accessing an S3 object. Format: https://[bucket-name].s3.[region].amazonaws.com/[key]. By default, returns Access Denied because objects are private.
terms.example: https://mycompany.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/logo.png

terms.definition: A method for uploading large files to S3 by splitting them into smaller parts, uploading in parallel, and having S3 reassemble them. Required for files over 5 GB.
terms.example: Uploading a 20 GB database dump: S3 splits it into 4 parts of 5 GB each, uploads all 4 simultaneously, then reassembles into a single object.

terms.definition: The default S3 storage class for frequently accessed data. Stores data across 3+ AZs, millisecond access, no retrieval fee, highest cost per GB.
terms.example: Hosting images for an active e-commerce website where users access product photos daily.

terms.definition: Infrequent Access storage class for data accessed monthly. Multi-AZ, millisecond retrieval, 128 KB minimum billable size, 30-day minimum duration, retrieval fee applies.
terms.example: Storing monthly financial reports that need to be retrieved quickly when requested but are only accessed once or twice a month.

terms.definition: Like Standard-IA but stored in a single AZ only. About 20% cheaper but at risk if the AZ fails. Not suitable for primary backups of irreplaceable data.
terms.example: Storing thumbnail images generated from originals — if lost, they can be regenerated from the original files.

terms.definition: A storage class that automatically monitors object access patterns and moves objects between tiers (Frequent, Infrequent, Archive) to optimize cost. Charges a per-object monitoring fee but no retrieval fee.
terms.example: Storing user-generated content with unpredictable access patterns — recent posts accessed daily, old posts rarely accessed.

terms.definition: Archive storage class for data accessed quarterly. Millisecond retrieval, 90-day minimum duration, retrieval fee applies. Lowest-cost option with instant access.
terms.example: Medical imaging archives accessed occasionally for patient follow-up appointments.

terms.definition: Archive storage class with retrieval times of 1–12 hours (standard) or 1–5 minutes (expedited, higher cost). 90-day minimum, for rarely accessed data.
terms.example: IT backup archives retrieved only when disaster recovery is triggered.

terms.definition: The lowest-cost S3 storage class. Designed for data retained 7–10 years with retrieval times up to 12–48 hours. 180-day minimum storage duration.
terms.example: Bank transaction records retained for 10 years for regulatory compliance, accessed only during audits.

terms.definition: An S3 feature that preserves multiple versions of the same object. Each upload of the same key creates a new version; old versions are retained and can be restored.
terms.example: Uploading an updated configuration file — versioning keeps the previous config in case the new one causes issues.

terms.definition: A placeholder S3 creates when an object is deleted from a versioning-enabled bucket. The object hides from the main view but all versions remain. Removing the marker restores the object.
terms.example: Accidentally deleting a report from S3 — the delete marker hides it, but removing the marker instantly restores it.

terms.definition: A feature that prevents objects from being deleted or overwritten for a defined retention period using a WORM (Write Once Read Many) model.
terms.example: A financial institution locking transaction records so no one can alter them during a 7-year retention period.

terms.definition: A data storage principle where, once written, data cannot be overwritten or deleted for a defined period. S3 implements this through Object Lock.
terms.example: SEC-regulated financial firms use WORM to comply with data retention regulations.

terms.definition: An S3 Object Lock retention mode where NO user — including the root account — can delete or modify the locked object until the retention period expires.
terms.example: Healthcare companies using Compliance mode to meet HIPAA requirements for patient record immutability.

terms.definition: An S3 Object Lock retention mode that prevents most users from modifying or deleting objects, but users with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention permission can override it.
terms.example: A content archive where admins retain the ability to correct accidental data errors while protecting against general user deletions.

terms.definition: An S3 Object Lock setting that prevents deletion without a fixed retention period. Stays active indefinitely until explicitly removed by a user with s3:PutObjectLegalHold permission.
terms.example: Placing a legal hold on all records related to an ongoing lawsuit, ensuring no documents can be deleted until the case is resolved.

terms.definition: 99.999999999% durability — the guarantee that stored objects will not be lost. Achieved by replicating data across multiple devices and facilities within a region.
terms.example: If you store 10 million objects in S3, you can expect to lose at most 0.0000001 of them in a year — statistically near zero.

terms.definition: The smallest size S3 will charge for an object, regardless of actual file size. Applies to IA classes (128 KB) — a 1 KB file in Standard-IA is billed as 128 KB.
terms.example: Storing 1,000 tiny 2 KB config files in Standard-IA costs as much as storing 1,000 files of 128 KB each.
